title: The mathematics, step by step
intro: Open a topic for the formula, its meaning and a worked example. These explain the implemented methods, not proof of a health effect.
associationExplanation: Pearson compares paired deviations from each variable’s mean. Spearman uses ranks instead. A relationship can reflect a third variable: a demanding week might change both stress and sleep. Neither coefficient identifies an intervention’s effect.
associationFormula: r = Σ[(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ)] / √[Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² × Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)²]
associationSymbols: xᵢ and yᵢ are observations paired by calendar date and the chosen lag; bars denote means. A constant variable makes the denominator zero, so the coefficient is undefined. Missing pairs are excluded, never replaced by zero.
associationExample: Example: r = −0.8 means a strong negative linear association in the selected pairs, not “80% less sleep”. Monday evening habits pair with Tuesday’s sleep at lag 1 because sleep belongs to its waking date.
bayesExplanation: The likelihood describes observations under a linear model with Gaussian noise. The prior shrinks coefficients toward zero. Combining them gives a posterior distribution, not a single certain answer. The app uses a Normal–Inverse-Gamma prior and calculates the posterior analytically.
bayesFormula: Vₙ = (V₀⁻¹ + XᵀX)⁻¹; mₙ = VₙXᵀz; aₙ = 2 + n/2
bayesSymbols: X is the design matrix, z the normalized outcome, n the complete rows and mₙ the posterior coefficient mean. V₀ has intercept scale 10 and slope scale 10, 1 or 0.1 for weak, regular or strong shrinkage. Residual variance has prior InverseGamma(2, 1). These are modeling choices, not healthy population targets.
bayesExample: Example: a coefficient of −0.2 sleep hours per stress point describes the fitted association with other selected inputs held fixed. It does not show that reducing stress by one point will cause 12 extra minutes of sleep.
uncertaintyExplanation: The mean band describes uncertainty about the modeled average. The predictive band also includes variation between individual observations. Both are equal-tailed 95% Student-t intervals conditional on the data, prior and model assumptions.
uncertaintySymbols: x* is the new input row; aₙ and bₙ are posterior residual parameters. These are squared Student-t scales, not variances. Bounds use the 0.975 quantile with 2aₙ degrees of freedom and return to outcome units. The additional 1 explains the wider predictive band.
uncertaintyExample: Example: a narrow band around an average of 7 hours can coexist with a wide range for one future night. Longer extrapolation cannot anticipate illness or a changed routine. Serially correlated errors can make the displayed bands too optimistic.
validationExplanation: The last 20% of outcome dates form a chronological holdout. Training outcomes must precede the first holdout input date. MAE measures typical absolute error; interval score penalizes both width and missed observations. Smaller scores are better only for comparable outcomes, dates and horizons.
validationFormula: IS₉₅ = (u − l) + 40 × max(l − y, 0) + 40 × max(y − u, 0)
validationSymbols: l and u are the lower and upper 95% predictive bounds; y is the later observation. The penalty multiplier is 2/0.05 = 40. Scores are averaged over the same held-out dates. An empty or too-small holdout does not produce a validation claim.
validationExample: Example: interval [6, 8] with observation 7 scores 2; with observation 9 it scores 42. Merely widening every interval has a cost. Repeatedly tuning settings after seeing test scores can overfit the holdout itself.
reviewTitle: 5. An unusual entry is a question, not an error
reviewExplanation: The entry review uses at least 30 earlier comparable measurements within 90 days. Its robust band uses the median and median absolute deviation (MAD), with a scale floor for stable or rounded histories. This is a review heuristic, separate from Bayesian forecasts.
reviewFormula: spread = max(MAD / 0.67448975, floor); band = median ± 3.5 × spread
reviewSymbols: MAD is the median of absolute distances from the median. The floor is one quarter of the metric’s modeling scale, 1 event for counts, or 5 minutes for habit duration. Separate relationship checks use stability gates and a nominal 99.5% regression prediction interval; their assumptions and thresholds are in the full specification.
reviewExample: Example: median 10 and spread 2 give a band from 3 to 17. An entry of 18 asks for review, but you can keep it. The band is not a healthy range; genuine changes are not corrected or excluded. No notice does not guarantee correctness.
limits: Named sources support methods, not clinical validation of this service. Missingness, correlated errors, multiple comparisons and changing routines can weaken the results. Demo associations are synthetic.
specification: Full model specification, assumptions & named references
dictionaryHelp: Open only the categories you need. Search opens matching groups, including sports; no scrolling through the entire activity catalog is needed.
